title: Functions 101 — Write Once, Use Everywhere
description: The DRY principle in action. Stop copying code. Learn to write reusable functions.
learningObjectives: I can explain what a function is and why it exists
I can write a function with parameters and a return value
I can identify when repeated code should become a function

contentSections.body: Marcus spent 3 hours building a tip calculator. Then he needed the same logic on 4 different screens. He copied and pasted the code 4 times. Then he found a bug. He had to fix it in 5 places. There's a better way.

**DRY** stands for *Don't Repeat Yourself*. It's one of the most important principles in coding.

Every time you copy-paste code, you're creating a future maintenance nightmare. When you find a bug (and you will), you have to fix it in every copy.

**Functions solve this.** A function is a named block of code that you can call from anywhere. Write it once, use it everywhere.

contentSections.answer: If the tip rate changes (or you find a bug), you have to update it in every place. Miss one and the behavior is inconsistent.
contentSections.hint: Think about what happens when you need to change the tip percentage

contentSections.body: If you're about to copy code for the second time — stop. That's your signal to write a function.
**Arrow functions** are the modern syntax. `const calculateTip = (bill, rate = 0.18) => { ... }` — same behavior, cleaner look. Both work; arrow functions are more common in modern codebases.

contentSections.question: What does a function without a `return` statement return?
contentSections.answer: `undefined`. Every function returns something. If you don't specify a return value, JavaScript returns `undefined` by default.
contentSections.hint: Think about what happens when nothing is explicitly returned

contentSections.body: A function takes inputs (parameters), does work, and returns an output. Parameters → transformation → return value.

contentSections.question: calculateTip is called with only one argument. What rate does it use?

options.label: 0 (no tip)
0.18 (the default)

feedback.default: Right — rate has a default value of 0.18, used whenever no second argument is passed.
feedback.zero: Not quite — JavaScript doesn't silently default a missing parameter to 0. It uses whatever default value you wrote (0.18 here).

contentSections.concept: `(bill, rate = 0.18)` — parameters are inputs the function receives. `= 0.18` is a default value used automatically when no argument is passed for that parameter.

title: Parameters, Return Values & Scope
description: Go deeper on how data flows into and out of functions. Understand why variables in functions don't leak out.
learningObjectives: I can explain the difference between parameters and arguments
I can use default parameters effectively
I can explain what scope means and why it matters

contentSections.body: Alex builds AI pipelines where the same function processes thousands of different messages. Each message is different — the function needs to handle all of them. Parameters make that possible.

contentSections.question: What happens if you call `greet('Sarah')` — without the age argument?
contentSections.answer: `age` will be `undefined`, and the output is 'Hi Sarah, you're undefined!' — no error, just unexpected output. This is why default parameters exist.
contentSections.hint: JavaScript doesn't throw an error for missing arguments — what does it fill in instead?

contentSections.body: Parameters are placeholders. Arguments are real values. Missing arguments become `undefined` — use defaults to prevent silent bugs.

contentSections.question: When is destructuring in parameters most useful?
contentSections.answer: When a function takes an object with many properties — instead of listing 5+ parameters, you destructure the object and pull out only what you need. Much cleaner than `(user.name, user.role, user.active)`.
contentSections.hint: Think about functions that take an object with many properties

contentSections.body: Default parameters prevent `undefined` surprises. Destructuring in parameters cleans up object-heavy functions.

contentSections.question: What happens on the last line?

options.label: Prints 'I only exist inside this function'
ReferenceError: localMessage is not defined

feedback.error: Right — localMessage is local to doSomething(). It disappears once the function ends, so nothing outside can see it.
feedback.prints: Not quite — variables declared inside a function are local. They don't exist outside it at all, not even the value from the last call.

contentSections.concept: Variables declared inside a function are local — they disappear when the function ends. This is good: it prevents functions from accidentally overwriting each other's data.

contentSections.body: **Scope bug:** If you forget `const` or `let`, JavaScript creates a global variable by accident — accessible everywhere. Always declare variables explicitly.

title: Reading Error Messages
description: Errors aren't failures — they're messages. Learn to decode what JavaScript is actually telling you.
learningObjectives: I can identify the type of error from an error message
I can find the file and line number where an error occurred
I can fix the 3 most common JavaScript errors

contentSections.body: Every new developer panics when they see a red error message. But here's the secret: the error message is trying to help you. It's JavaScript's way of saying 'here's exactly what went wrong, and here's where.'

A JavaScript error message has three parts:

```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')
    at getUserName (app.js:14:22)
    at main (app.js:8:5)
```

1. **Error type** (`TypeError`) — the category of error
2. **Error message** — what went wrong in plain English
3. **Stack trace** — which file, which line, which function called what

**Common error types:**
- `ReferenceError` — you used a variable that doesn't exist
- `TypeError` — you used a value in a way its type doesn't support
- `SyntaxError` — your code can't even be parsed (usually a missing bracket or semicolon)
- `RangeError` — a number is outside a valid range

contentSections.question: `ReferenceError: userName is not defined` — What probably happened?
contentSections.answer: You tried to use `userName` but either forgot to declare it (`const userName = ...`) or misspelled it (maybe it's `username` lowercase).
contentSections.hint: The error says 'is not defined' — what could cause a variable to not exist?

contentSections.body: Read errors top to bottom: type → message → first line of the stack trace. The stack trace tells you exactly where to look.

**1. Cannot read properties of undefined**
```js
const user = undefined;
console.log(user.name); // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
```
Fix: Check if the value exists first: `if (user) { console.log(user.name); }`

**2. is not a function**
```js
const count = 5;
count.map(x => x * 2); // TypeError: count.map is not a function
```
Fix: `map` is an array method. `count` is a number. Check your data type.

**3. Unexpected token / missing bracket**
```js
const add = (a, b => { // SyntaxError
  return a + b;
}
```
Fix: Missing `)` before `=>`. Read carefully around the line number.

contentSections.question:
What does this error mean?
`TypeError: fetch is not a function`
contentSections.answer: You're probably running this code in Node.js (not a browser). `fetch` is a browser API. In older versions of Node.js, it doesn't exist. Solution: import it with `node-fetch` or use Node 18+ which has built-in fetch.
contentSections.hint: fetch is a web browser API — where might it not exist?

contentSections.body: Most errors fall into 3 buckets: variable doesn't exist, wrong data type, or syntax mistake. 90% of bugs are one of these.

contentSections.question: What error type does this throw?

options.label: ReferenceError
TypeError

feedback.type: Right — map is an array method; count is a number. Using a value in a way its type doesn't support is exactly what TypeError means.
feedback.ref: Not quite — count IS defined, so it's not a missing-variable error. The problem is that a number doesn't have a .map method, which is a TypeError.

contentSections.concept: TypeError — you used a value in a way its type doesn't support. count.map is not a function, because map is an array method and count is a number.

contentSections.body:
When you're stuck, Claude is your rubber duck. But how you ask matters.

**Bad prompt:**
> 'My code doesn't work, fix it'

**Good prompt:**
> 'I'm getting this error: `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'price')` on line 23 of checkout.js. Here's the relevant code: [paste 10-20 lines]. The error happens when I try to access the cart items. What's wrong?'

The magic formula: **Error message + relevant code + what you expected vs. what happened**.

Claude will identify the bug, explain why it happened, and suggest a fix. More importantly, it'll help you understand the pattern — so you recognize it next time.

**console.log is your friend.** Before asking Claude, add `console.log()` before the error line to inspect the value. Often you'll see the problem immediately: 'Oh, it's undefined because the API hasn't loaded yet.'

title: Debugging Strategies That Actually Work
description: rubber duck debugging, console.log patterns, binary search debugging. Build a systematic debugging toolkit.
learningObjectives: I can narrow down a bug using binary search debugging
I can use console.log strategically to inspect state
I can explain what rubber duck debugging is and when to use it

contentSections.body: Sarah has a function with 30 lines. Something's wrong but the error is vague. She could read every line carefully (slow). Or she could cut the problem in half: comment out lines 15-30 and test again. If it works, the bug is in lines 15-30. If it still fails, the bug is in lines 1-15. Keep halving until you find it.

**Binary search debugging** is the most efficient strategy:

1. Identify the broken behavior
2. Find the midpoint of the suspicious code
3. Add a checkpoint (console.log) there
4. Does the code reach the checkpoint with correct data? If yes → bug is after. If no → bug is before.
5. Repeat until you isolate the exact line

This works because each step cuts the search space in half.

contentSections.scenario: Sarah has a 30-line function with a vague bug. Binary search checks the midpoint, then narrows to ~15 lines, then ~8, then ~4, then ~2 — until she finds it. Most developers instead check line by line, one at a time.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many times faster is binary search than checking line-by-line?
contentSections.explanation: 30 lines → 15 → 8 → 4 → 2 → found — each step cuts the search space in half. Most developers brute-force, checking line by line; binary search is roughly 5× faster.

contentSections.question: A 100-line function has a bug. With binary search debugging, what's the maximum number of checkpoints you need to find it?
contentSections.answer: About 7. Each step halves the search space: 100 → 50 → 25 → 13 → 7 → 4 → 2 → 1. log₂(100) ≈ 7.
contentSections.hint: Each console.log cuts the problem in half. How many times can you halve 100?

contentSections.body: Don't read every line — narrow the problem space. Binary search debugging finds any bug in log₂(n) steps.

contentSections.question: Why is `console.log('user:', JSON.stringify(user, null, 2))` better than just `console.log('user:', user)` for complex objects?
contentSections.answer: When you `console.log` an object, browsers/Node show a live reference — so if the object mutates later, the logged value changes too (confusing!). JSON.stringify captures the value at that exact moment.
contentSections.hint: Objects in console.log are 'live' references — what might that cause?

contentSections.body: Label your logs. Use JSON.stringify for objects. Use console.table for arrays. Remove all debug logs before shipping.

contentSections.title: Rubber duck debugging + knowing when to ask

contentSections.body:
**Rubber duck debugging:** Explain your code out loud to an imaginary rubber duck (or Claude). The act of explaining forces you to think through each step — and often reveals the bug before you even finish explaining.

*'Okay, so first I get the user... then I get their cart... then I... wait, what if the cart is empty? I never check for that.'*

**When to ask Claude:**
- You've tried binary search and isolated the bug to 5 lines
- You've read the error message and still don't understand it
- You've spent 15+ minutes on the same bug

Don't ask immediately — the attempt to debug yourself builds pattern recognition. But don't suffer for hours either. Claude is a tool; use it strategically.
**The 15-minute rule:** Try to solve a bug yourself for 15 minutes. If you're still stuck, ask Claude. This ratio builds skills (you learn from attempts) while preventing endless frustration.

title: Thinking in Algorithms
description: An algorithm is just a recipe. Learn to break any problem into clear, ordered steps a computer can follow.
learningObjectives: I can explain what an algorithm is in plain English
I can break a real-world task into numbered steps
I can identify where a step is too vague and needs to be broken down further

contentSections.body: Every morning you make coffee. You probably don't think about it as an algorithm. But it is: boil water → measure coffee → pour into filter → wait → pour into cup → drink. That's an algorithm. Coding is the same idea — you're just writing the recipe in a language a computer understands.

An **algorithm** is a finite, ordered sequence of steps that solves a problem.

The key properties:
- **Finite** — it must end at some point
- **Ordered** — the sequence matters
- **Unambiguous** — each step must be clear enough to execute

When new developers start coding, they often try to write code immediately. The better approach:
1. Describe the solution in plain English
2. Break it into numbered steps
3. Check: is each step something a computer can do?
4. *Then* translate to code

Claude can help with step 3-4. You need to do steps 1-2 yourself — that's the thinking part.

contentSections.question: Break this into algorithm steps: 'Find the most expensive item in a shopping cart'
contentSections.answer:
1. Start with the first item as the 'current most expensive'
2. For each remaining item: compare its price to the current most expensive
3. If the new item costs more, it becomes the new 'current most expensive'
4. After checking all items, return the 'current most expensive'
contentSections.hint: Think step by step — how would you do this by hand with a list on paper?

contentSections.body: Write the algorithm in English before writing code. If you can't explain the steps in English, you can't write them in code.

**Decomposition** means breaking a complex problem into simpler sub-problems.

Example: 'Build a checkout system'

That's too big. Break it down:
- Validate the cart (has items, quantities > 0)
- Calculate total price
- Apply any discounts
- Process payment
- Update inventory
- Send confirmation email

Each of those is still complex. Break them down further:

'Apply any discounts' →
- Check if user has a promo code
- Look up promo code in database
- If valid and not expired, calculate discount amount
- Apply discount to total

Keep breaking down until each step is a single, testable function.

**Ask Claude to help you decompose.** 'I need to build X. Help me break this into the 5-8 high-level steps I need to implement.' Claude is excellent at this — it's essentially mapping your problem against thousands of similar patterns it's seen.

contentSections.question: What's the difference between an algorithm and code?
contentSections.answer: An algorithm is the idea — the logic described in any language (English, pseudocode, diagrams). Code is the implementation of that idea in a specific programming language. The algorithm comes first; the code expresses it.
contentSections.hint: Think about whether you could describe an algorithm in Spanish or on a whiteboard

contentSections.body: Decompose any big problem into smaller pieces. Each piece should be simple enough to write as a single function.

contentSections.title: Pattern recognition — solving the same problem differently

contentSections.scenario: You need to combine every item's price into one running total.
contentSections.question: Which pattern is this?

options.label: Transform
Accumulate

feedback.accumulate: Right — combining items into one value is Accumulate (.reduce() or a running total), not Transform.
feedback.transform: Not quite — Transform converts each item into a new form but still gives you one output per input. Combining everything into a single total is Accumulate.

contentSections.concept: Search — find an item that matches criteria. Sort — arrange items in order. Transform — convert each item to something new. Accumulate — combine items into one value. Filter — keep only items matching criteria. Most real problems are combinations of 2-3 of these.

contentSections.body:
Experienced developers recognize that most problems are variations of a small number of patterns:

**Search** — find an item that matches criteria (use `.find()` or `.filter()`)
**Sort** — arrange items in order (use `.sort()`)
**Transform** — convert each item to something new (use `.map()`)
**Accumulate** — combine items into one value (use `.reduce()` or a for loop with a running total)
**Filter** — keep only items matching criteria (use `.filter()`)

When you see a new problem, ask: *is this fundamentally a search, sort, transform, accumulate, or filter?*

Most real problems are combinations of 2-3 of these patterns.

title: Arrays & Objects — Working with Data
description: Real apps have lists of things. Learn to create, read, update, and delete data in arrays and objects.
learningObjectives: I can use CRUD operations on arrays and objects
I can choose between an array and an object for a given use case
I can write code that processes a list of items

contentSections.body: Every real app has lists: a list of users, a list of messages, a list of products. If you can work with arrays, you can work with data. That's most of what apps do.

contentSections.question: What's the difference between `.push()` and `.concat()`?
contentSections.answer: `.push()` modifies the original array and returns the new length. `.concat()` returns a new array without modifying the original. In modern JS, prefer `[...arr, newItem]` (spread syntax) which also returns a new array.
contentSections.hint: Think about whether the original array changes

contentSections.body: Arrays hold ordered lists. Use `.filter()`, `.map()`, `.find()` for non-destructive operations. Use `.push()` when you want to mutate.

contentSections.question: You have a list of 1000 users. You often need to look up a specific user by ID. Should you store them as an array or as an object keyed by ID?
contentSections.answer: Object keyed by ID. With an array, finding user with ID 487 requires scanning up to 1000 items. With an object `{487: user}`, lookup is instant (O(1)). This is a fundamental data structure tradeoff.
contentSections.hint: Think about how fast you can find something in a list vs. a dictionary

contentSections.body: Use objects when you need to look things up by name or ID. Use arrays when order matters or you need to iterate over all items.

contentSections.title: Arrays of objects — the real-world pattern

contentSections.question: What's the value of total?
contentSections.explanation: 45×1 + 120×1 + 15×3 = 45 + 120 + 45 = 210. reduce() walks the array once, adding each item's price×qty onto a running sum that starts at 0.

title: A variable is a name for a value
description: A variable is a named place to store a value you can look up and change later — not the value itself, frozen in place.

learningObjectives.text: Explain that a variable is a name pointing at a current value, not the value itself
Create a variable with `let` and read it back with console.log
Predict a variable's value after a reassignment

contentSections.title: A label, not a locked-in value

contentSections.body: You wake up with a fixed amount of energy today — call it 12 spoons. By 11am, getting through a shower and breakfast has cost you 4. If nothing is tracking the current number, by 3pm you're just guessing how much is left.

contentSections.scenario:
Three ways to track today's spoon count as the day goes on: a sticky note reading "Spoons: 12" that you erase and rewrite each time you spend some, trying to keep the whole day's math in your head, and this line of code:

```
let spoons = 12;
```
contentSections.question: Which of these is closest to what a variable in code actually does?

options.label: The sticky note you erase and rewrite
Keeping the running total in your head
They're all the same thing, functionally

feedback.note: Right. One named spot ("Spoons:") holding a current value that gets erased and rewritten as it changes — that's exactly what a variable is. The label stays the same; what it points at changes.
feedback.head: Mental tracking has no fixed "place" at all — nothing to look up later, nothing another line of code (or another day of you) could check reliably. A variable needs to be something checkable, not just remembered.
feedback.same: They're not equivalent — the mental version has no durable, checkable place to look, which is exactly the property a variable needs and a memory doesn't reliably have.

contentSections.concept: A variable is a named place to store a value that can be looked up and changed later. The name (`spoons`) doesn't hold the number physically glued to it — it points at whatever the current value is, the same way "Spoons:" on the sticky note points at whatever's currently written next to it.

contentSections.body:
In code that's written as:

```
let spoons = 12;
console.log(spoons); // 12
spoons = spoons - 4;
console.log(spoons); // 8
```

`let spoons = 12;` does two things at once: it creates a variable named `spoons`, and gives it a starting value of 12. `console.log(spoons)` looks up whatever `spoons` currently points at and prints it. The `=` here is **assignment** — "make this name point at this value" — not the equals sign from math class, even though it looks identical. `spoons = spoons - 4` reads the current value, subtracts 4, and makes `spoons` point at the result instead.
A variable is a name you can look up and reassign — not a value glued in place.

contentSections.title: Each reassignment uses whatever came before it

contentSections.body: By evening you've spent spoons three separate times today. Whatever's left now depends on every deduction that already happened — not just the number you started with this morning.

contentSections.hint: Update `spoons` one line at a time. What is it after line 2, before line 3 even runs?
contentSections.answer: 5. After line 1, spoons is 12. After line 2, it's 12 − 4 = 8. After line 3, it's 8 − 3 = 5 — each line subtracts from whatever spoons currently holds at that exact moment, not from the original 12. The final console.log only ever sees the last value it was pointed at.

contentSections.body: This is the same top-to-bottom rule that runs the whole program: each line does its work using whatever the variable currently holds, in the order the lines actually run. `spoons = spoons - 4` isn't circular even though `spoons` appears on both sides — the right-hand side is calculated first, using the *old* value, and only then does `spoons` get reassigned to the result. Every reassignment after that starts from whatever the previous line left behind.
Every reassignment starts from whatever the variable currently holds, not from its original value.

title: Numbers, text and true/false: the three you need first
description: The three types that carry almost every beginner program: numbers for arithmetic, strings for text, and booleans for yes/no — and the quotes that decide which one you actually have.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a number, a string and a boolean by how each is written
Explain why quotes change a value's type even when the characters look numeric
Predict whether a comparison between differently-typed values is true or false

contentSections.title: The same digits, two different things

contentSections.body: You log today's pain level as 4. Later you log today's medication as "400mg". Both involve a 4 — but one of them you can do arithmetic on, and one of them you very much cannot, and JavaScript needs to know which is which before it does anything with either.

contentSections.question: Which of these four is a number, in JavaScript's terms?

options.label: painLevel (4, no quotes)
doseLabel ("400mg", in quotes)
medName ("ibuprofen", in quotes)

feedback.painLevel: Right — no quotes, and it's a plain digit. That's what makes it a number JavaScript can do arithmetic with.
feedback.doseLabel: It contains digits, but the quotes make the whole thing text — "400mg" is a label to display, not a value to calculate with. The letters "mg" tucked inside are actually a strong hint it was never meant to be math.
feedback.medName: This one has no digits at all, but the deciding factor is still the quotes — anything inside quotes is a string, full stop, regardless of what characters are in it.

contentSections.concept: A number is written with no quotes: `4`, `3.5`, `-12`. A string (text) is anything inside quotes, single or double: `"4"`, `"400mg"`, `"ibuprofen"` — even a string that's entirely digits is still text, not a number, as far as JavaScript is concerned.

contentSections.body:
JavaScript has a handful of basic types, and three of them cover almost everything a beginner program needs:

- **Number** — `4`, `3.5`, `-12`. No quotes. Can be added, subtracted, compared with `<` and `>`.
- **String** — `"hello"`, `"400mg"`, `"4"`. Quoted text. Even digits in quotes are text, not numbers.
- **Boolean** — `true` or `false`. No quotes, and nothing else counts — `"true"` in quotes is a string that happens to spell the word.

You can check a value's type directly with `typeof`: `typeof 4` is `"number"`, `typeof "4"` is `"string"`, `typeof true` is `"boolean"`.
Quotes decide the type. "4" and 4 look almost identical and are completely different things to JavaScript.

contentSections.title: Booleans are exactly two values, spelled exactly one way

contentSections.body: A symptom tracker asks: did you take your meds today? There are only ever two honest answers to that — which is exactly what a boolean is for.

contentSections.scenario: A form is meant to store whether someone took their medication today, as a boolean.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually store a real boolean value?

explanation.bare_true: Yes — the bare word `true`, no quotes, is the actual boolean value.
explanation.bare_false: Yes — same reasoning, `false` with no quotes is the other (and only other) real boolean value.
explanation.quoted_true: This is a three-letter string that spells "true" — it prints the same as the real thing but has a completely different type (`typeof` would say `"string"`, not `"boolean"`), which can quietly break comparisons and logic later.
explanation.num_one: 1 is a real, valid number — sometimes used elsewhere to represent "yes" — but it is not literally a boolean in JavaScript. `typeof 1` says `"number"`.

contentSections.synthesis: There are exactly two real boolean values in JavaScript — bare `true` and bare `false` — and nothing else, no matter how closely it resembles them, actually is one.

contentSections.body: Booleans matter beyond just storing yes/no answers — they're what conditions produce. `4 > 2` evaluates to the boolean `true`. `age === ageText` from the first pod evaluates to the boolean `false`. Every comparison in JavaScript produces one of exactly these two values, which is why getting comfortable with `true` and `false` as real values now — not just as words — pays off the moment conditions show up.
There are exactly two real booleans, spelled exactly one way each: bare true, bare false.

title: Names that tell the next reader what this is
description: JavaScript accepts almost any valid name — the discipline of picking a specific, honest one is entirely on you, and it's what saves the next reader (often you) from having to reverse-engineer the code to understand it.

learningObjectives.text: State the rules that make a variable name valid in JavaScript
Distinguish a valid name from a good, specific one
Rewrite a vague variable name to say what it actually holds

contentSections.body: You try `let 2ndDose = "9am";` and the whole program refuses to run, before a single line of it does anything — not because the idea was wrong, but because of one character at the very start of the name.

contentSections.scenario:
This line causes JavaScript to reject the file outright, before running anything:

```
let 2ndDose = "9am";
```
contentSections.question: What's actually wrong with this line?

options.label: "2ndDose" isn't descriptive enough
Variable names can't start with a digit
"9am" should be a number, not text

feedback.vague: Actually this name is quite descriptive — that's not the issue here. This is a hard rule violation, not a style problem.
feedback.digit: Right. JavaScript variable names may contain digits, but can't start with one — `2ndDose` starts with `2`, which the parser can't accept as the beginning of a name.
feedback.quotes: "9am" is a legitimate string — a time written as text is completely fine. That's not what's breaking this line.

contentSections.mechanism: A variable name has to start with a letter, `$`, or `_` — never a digit. This isn't about the name being bad; it's a hard rule the parser enforces before it even looks at what the line is trying to do. Renaming it to `doseTwoTime` (or similar) fixes it instantly, with no other change needed.

contentSections.body: The actual rules are short: a name can contain letters, digits, `$` and `_`, but can't start with a digit, and can't contain spaces. JavaScript is case-sensitive too — `doseCount` and `dosecount` are two entirely different variables, not the same one written two ways. The near-universal convention is **camelCase**: lowercase for the first word, capitalize the start of each word after that — `spoonsRemaining`, `doseCount`, `isLoggedIn`. Nothing forces this convention, but almost all JavaScript you'll ever read uses it, so following it makes your code look like everyone else's.
A name must start with a letter, `$`, or `_` — never a digit — and can't contain spaces.

contentSections.title: Valid isn't the same as useful

contentSections.body: `let x = 12;` runs perfectly. So does `let spoonsRemaining = 12;`. JavaScript is completely indifferent between them — the difference only shows up for whoever reads this file three weeks from now with no memory of today.

contentSections.question: You open a file you wrote a month ago and find `let d = 4;` with no comment nearby. What's the actual cost of a name like `d`?
contentSections.hint: The cost isn't about whether the program runs — it already does. Think about what has to happen before you can safely change this line.
contentSections.answer: Before you can safely touch this line, you have to go read the surrounding code to reconstruct what `d` actually means — dose? day? distance? A specific name like `doseMg` or `daysElapsed` would have answered that instantly, on sight, with zero extra reading. The cost of a vague name isn't paid when it's written; it's paid every single time it's read again.

contentSections.body: A genuinely good variable name states what the value *is*, specifically enough that you wouldn't need to guess: `painLevel` instead of `p`, `medsTakenToday` instead of `flag`, `spoonsRemaining` instead of `data`. Short names like `i` are a real, accepted exception in one specific place — counting through a small loop — because their scope is tiny and their meaning is obvious in context; outside that, shortness stops being a virtue and starts being a cost paid by every future reader, including you.
A name doesn't have to be long to be good — it has to answer "what is this?" without making anyone go looking.

title: Type errors and "2" plus 2
description: JavaScript rarely stops a program to complain about mismatched types — it quietly converts one type into another instead, and knowing exactly when it does that is what turns a confusing wrong answer into a predictable one.

learningObjectives.text: Predict the result of `+` between a string and a number
Explain why `-`, `*` and `/` behave differently from `+` with mixed types
Recognise form and API input as a common real-world source of unexpected string values

contentSections.title: The most famous surprise in JavaScript

contentSections.body: You build a simple age-next-year calculator. It compiles, it runs, nothing throws an error — and the number on screen is wrong in a way that took you twenty confused minutes to even notice, because the program never told you anything went wrong.

contentSections.question: This runs with no error, but doesn't print 33. What's actually going on?

options.label: There's a typo in the variable name
`age` is text ("32"), so `+` glues it to `1` as text instead of adding
`console.log` can only print numbers, not the result of `+`

feedback.typo: No typo here — every name is spelled consistently and used correctly. The bug is about type, not spelling.
feedback.coercion: Right. `age` holds the string "32" (it arrived from a form field, which are text by default). `+` between a string and a number glues them together as text, producing "321", not the sum 33.
feedback.logbug: `console.log` prints whatever value it's handed, whatever type that value is — it isn't restricted to numbers. The problem happened before `console.log` was ever called.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This runs without a single error message, which is exactly what makes it dangerous — a wrong value slips through silently instead of stopping the program to flag it. The fix is to convert the text to a real number before doing arithmetic on it, which the next lesson covers directly.

contentSections.body: This behavior has a name: **type coercion** — JavaScript automatically converting one type into another to make an operation "work," instead of stopping with an error. `+` is the operator most notorious for it, because `+` has two entirely different jobs depending on what it's given: add two numbers, or join two strings. If *either* side of `+` is a string, JavaScript picks the joining behavior — even if the string looks entirely numeric, like `"32"`.
If either side of `+` is a string, JavaScript joins as text — even if that string is all digits.

contentSections.title: Other operators don't play by the same rule

contentSections.body: The exact same kind of mixed-up value — a number that arrived as text — behaves completely differently the moment you switch from `+` to `-`. Same mistake, different symptom, which is exactly what makes this genuinely confusing the first time.

contentSections.hint: Only `+` has a "join as text" meaning. `*`, like `-` and `/`, only ever means one thing: the math operation.
contentSections.answer: It prints 6, not "33" and not an error. `*`, `-`, and `/` have no "join text" meaning to fall back on — they only mean arithmetic — so JavaScript converts the string "3" into the number 3 first, then multiplies: 3 × 2 = 6. This is the opposite-feeling behavior from `+`, and it's genuinely one rule, not two: `+` is the only operator that treats a string specially, because it's the only one with a text-joining meaning to offer instead.

contentSections.body: So the actual rule is narrower than "JavaScript is weird about types": `+` is genuinely special, because it's overloaded to mean two different things (add or join) depending on what it's given, and a string tips it toward joining. `-`, `*`, and `/` have no second meaning to offer — they only ever mean arithmetic — so a numeric-looking string gets silently converted to a real number first instead. Knowing this one distinction is most of what it takes to stop being surprised by mixed-type arithmetic.
`+` is the one operator with a text-joining alternative meaning — that's the entire reason it behaves differently from `-`, `*` and `/`.

title: Converting between types on purpose
description: Instead of hoping an operator will happen to convert a value the way you want, JavaScript gives you explicit functions to do it deliberately — and one genuine trap in the boolean version worth knowing about upfront.

learningObjectives.text: Convert a numeric-looking string into a real number with Number(...)
Convert a value into text with String(...) or template literals
Recognise the trap in converting a string to a boolean with Boolean(...)

contentSections.body: Lesson 4 showed what happens when a numeric-looking string sneaks into arithmetic by accident. This pod is about doing that same conversion on purpose, so it happens exactly when and how you intend, not as a side effect of which operator you happened to use.

contentSections.scenario: A form field always returns text, even when someone types digits into it. To do real math on `"32"`, you need it as an actual number first.
contentSections.question: Which of these is the deliberate, reliable way to convert "32" into the number 32?

options.label: Number("32")
Just use "32" as-is in later math

feedback.number_fn: Right. `Number("32")` has one job — convert its argument into a real number — and it does that explicitly, in a way any reader can see was intentional.
feedback.plus_zero: This is the trap from lesson 4 in disguise: with a string on the left, `+` glues as text, so `"32" + 0` produces `"320"`, not 32. It looks like conversion but is actually the exact bug it's meant to avoid.
feedback.asis: This just delays the surprise — the first arithmetic operator that touches it will either silently coerce it (with `-`, `*`, `/`) or silently glue it as text (with `+`), and which one happens depends entirely on which operator you reach for.

contentSections.concept: `Number(value)` explicitly converts its argument into a number. It's the deliberate version of what `-`, `*`, and `/` do automatically behind the scenes — doing it on purpose, with a named function, means the conversion is visible in the code and doesn't depend on which operator happens to trigger it.

contentSections.body:
JavaScript gives you a function for each direction of conversion:

```
Number("32")     // 32 (a real number)
String(32)        // "32" (a real string)
Boolean(1)         // true
```

Going the other way — turning a value into text for display — is also commonly done with a **template literal**, backticks with `${...}` inside: `` `Age: ${age}` `` builds the string "Age: 32" without needing `String(...)` at all, and reads more clearly than gluing pieces together with `+`.
Number(...) and String(...) convert deliberately — don't rely on an operator to happen to do it for you.

contentSections.title: The one conversion that has a trap in it

contentSections.body: Number(...) and String(...) behave exactly the way they sound. Boolean(...) has one genuinely surprising rule hiding inside it, and it's specifically the kind of surprise that produces a bug which looks correct at first glance.

contentSections.question: What does this actually print, and which of the following explain why?

items.label: It prints true — even though the stored text says "false"
Boolean(...) treats any non-empty string as true, regardless of its content
Boolean(...) reads the word inside the string and matches it
It prints false, matching the stored text

explanation.prints_true: Correct, and it's the surprising part: `Boolean("false")` is `true`. The string "false" is non-empty, and that's the only thing `Boolean(...)` actually checks on a string.
explanation.nonempty: This is the real rule: `Boolean(...)` on a string only asks "is this empty or not" — `""` (empty) converts to `false`, and literally any other string, including `"false"`, converts to `true`.
explanation.reads_word: This is the tempting but wrong belief — it feels like `Boolean(...)` should be smart enough to read the word "false" and match it, but it genuinely doesn't inspect the string's content at all, only its length.
explanation.prints_false: This is what most people expect and exactly what doesn't happen — which is the whole reason this trap is worth knowing before you hit it in a real settings file.

contentSections.synthesis: The safe fix, from the exercise below, is to compare the stored text directly (`savedValue === "true"`) rather than trusting `Boolean(...)` to interpret it — `Boolean(...)` is genuinely the right tool for many things, but converting a "true"/"false" string isn't one of them.

contentSections.body: Boolean("false") is true. Boolean only checks whether a string is empty, never what it says.

title: Practice — Fix the Type Bug in Eight Snippets
description: Eight drills, no new concepts: reading a short snippet, predicting how JavaScript will handle its mixed types, and spotting exactly where a type-related bug is hiding.

learningObjectives.text: Predict how JavaScript converts mismatched types across common operators

contentSections.body: Every one of these traces back to the same handful of rules from this module: quotes mean text, `+` joins if either side is text, other operators convert to numbers, and Boolean(...) on a string only checks whether it's empty.
Almost every type surprise in this module comes down to one question: is there a quote mark you missed?

title: Lab — Model Something Real as a Set of Variables
description: Take something real from your own life and describe it in code as a set of well-named, correctly-typed variables — the first time this track asks you to model something, not just predict output.

learningObjectives.text: Choose an appropriate type (number, string, boolean) for each real value being modeled
Name each variable so its purpose is clear without a comment
Build a small working program from variables alone that prints a real, useful summary

contentSections.body: Every real thing you might track — a med schedule, a grocery order, a symptom log, a daily energy budget — is, underneath, a handful of individual values with names and types. This lab is about doing that translation deliberately, for something that's actually yours.

contentSections.title: Model a real thing as variables
contentSections.brief: Pick something from your own life you could describe as a small set of values: a daily spoon budget, a medication schedule, a grocery order, a symptom log entry, a reading list. This lab turns it into a real, running program — a set of correctly-typed, well-named variables that together describe the thing, plus a printed summary built from them.
contentSections.deliverable: A program describing a real object with well-named, correctly-typed variables.

stages.title: Pick the thing and list its values in plain English
stages.instructions: Choose one real thing to model. Write down, in plain English (no code yet), every individual value that describes it — for a medication: name, dose in mg, whether it's taken today, time due. Aim for 4-6 values. For each, note whether it's fundamentally a number, a piece of text, or a yes/no.
stages.checkpoint: You have 4-6 real values written down, each with a plain-English type guess (number, text, or yes/no).

stages.title: Turn each value into a correctly-typed variable
stages.instructions: Write one `let` line per value, using this lesson's rules: no quotes for numbers and booleans, quotes for text, camelCase names that state what each value is. Double-check every value's type against lesson 2 and 4 — a dose in mg should be a number, not `"400"` in quotes; whether it was taken should be a real boolean, not `"yes"`.
stages.checkpoint: Every variable uses the correct type for what it represents, and every name is specific enough to understand with no comment.

stages.title: Build one derived value from the others
stages.instructions: Add one more variable that's calculated from at least two of the others — spoons remaining after a planned activity, days until a refill is needed, total items in an order. This has to be real arithmetic on real numbers, so if any of your source values arrived as text (imagine they came from a form), convert them with Number(...) first, on purpose, the way lesson 5 covered.
stages.checkpoint: You have one calculated variable, built with a real arithmetic operator, using correctly-converted number values.

stages.title: Print a labeled summary and check it against the rubric
stages.instructions: Use console.log with a template literal to print a full sentence summarizing the thing you modeled, including the calculated value from stage 3 — not just the raw numbers, but something that reads like a real sentence a person would say. Run it and confirm the output is correct, then check your whole program against the rubric below before calling it done.
stages.checkpoint: The program runs and prints a complete, correctly-worded sentence with the right values in it, including the calculated one.

rubric.criterion: Every value has the correct type
rubric.meets: Numbers have no quotes, text is quoted, booleans are bare true/false — nothing modeled as the wrong type.

rubric.criterion: Every name is specific and readable
rubric.meets: A stranger reading just the variable names, no comments, could say what each one holds.

rubric.criterion: One value is genuinely calculated, not just typed in
rubric.meets: At least one variable is built from arithmetic on at least two others, using a real operator.

rubric.criterion: Any text-origin numbers are converted on purpose
rubric.meets: If a source value is imagined as arriving as text, it's explicitly passed through Number(...) before being used in math.

rubric.criterion: The program prints a real, readable summary
rubric.meets: console.log outputs a full sentence via a template literal, not just a bare number or an unlabeled value.

contentSections.body: Modeling something real as variables is the same skill as everything else this module covered — just aimed at your own life instead of a practice snippet.

title: Checkpoint — Variables and Types
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Asking an AI for Help, Well, two reaching back further into Starting From Nothing. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions, and earlier ones, without looking them up

questions.prompt: What does `let spoons = 12; spoons = 9;` leave `spoons` holding?

options.label: 12, since that's the original value
9 — the reassignment replaces the old value entirely
Both 12 and 9, kept separately

questions.explanation: A variable is a name pointing at a current value. Reassignment replaces what it points at — the old value isn't kept anywhere.

questions.prompt: Why does `"5" === 5` come out false in JavaScript?

options.label: === always returns false for numbers
One is a string and one is a number — different types, even with matching digits
5 needs a decimal point to count as a real number

questions.explanation: === checks type as well as value. "5" (a string) and 5 (a number) hold the "same" digits but are different types, so they're not equal.

options.label: The name isn't descriptive enough
A variable name can't start with a digit
"9am" should be a number, not text

questions.explanation: Names must start with a letter, $, or _ — never a digit. This is a hard parser rule, not a style suggestion.

options.label: + always converts to text when a number is nearby
With a string on either side, + joins as text instead of adding
1 is being treated as a string automatically for no reason

questions.explanation: + is uniquely overloaded to mean either addition or text-joining. A string on either side tips it toward joining, unlike -, *, or /.

questions.from: Previous module — Asking an AI for Help, Well
questions.prompt: From Asking an AI for Help, Well: what turns a generic AI answer into one that's actually about your specific bug?

options.label: Asking politely
Including the actual code, the actual error, and what you expected
Asking in as few words as possible

questions.explanation: An AI tool can't guess what it isn't told. The actual code, the actual error message, and your expected result are what make an answer specific instead of generic.

questions.from: Previous module — Asking an AI for Help, Well
questions.prompt: From Asking an AI for Help, Well: what's the real difference between asking for a fix versus asking for an explanation?

options.label: There's no real difference, both produce the same code
A fix changes tonight's file; an explanation changes what you can do next time
Explanations take longer to receive, nothing more

questions.explanation: A fix solves the immediate problem. An explanation builds the understanding that lets you solve the next similar one yourself.

questions.from: Previous module — Asking an AI for Help, Well
questions.prompt: From Asking an AI for Help, Well: what's a genuine, concrete way to check an AI's answer before trusting it, even without full understanding yet?

options.label: Trust it automatically if it sounds confident
Run it, compare the output to what you expected, and read the code line by line for anything that looks off
Only trust answers that include an apology for possible mistakes

questions.explanation: Confidence in tone tells you nothing about correctness. Running the code and reading it line by line are concrete, checkable signals.

questions.from: Previous module — Asking an AI for Help, Well
questions.prompt: From Asking an AI for Help, Well: what does pasting a working AI answer without reproducing it yourself train?

options.label: Recall — the ability to write it again from scratch
Recognition, not recall — which doesn't transfer to writing it yourself later
Nothing — pasting and typing build the same skill

questions.explanation: Recognizing a correct answer on screen is a different skill from generating it yourself. Deliberately reproducing it is what makes it stick.

questions.from: Three modules back — Errors Are Information
questions.prompt: From Errors Are Information: what are the three parts of a JavaScript error message?

options.label: A category, a description, and a location
A warning, an apology, and a suggestion
The file name, the date, and a severity score

questions.explanation: Category (what kind of error), description (what specifically went wrong), and location (where) — none of it is commentary on you as a person.

questions.from: Four modules back — What Code Actually Is
questions.prompt: From What Code Actually Is: in what order do a program's lines actually run?

options.label: Whichever order is most efficient
Top to bottom, one line at a time, in the order written
All at once

questions.explanation: One line at a time, top to bottom, with nothing simultaneous and no lookahead — the same rule that explains why a line can't use a variable created below it.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.
